title: feat(OpenAi Node): Add mTLS client certificate support
body:
## Summary

Adds mutual TLS (mTLS) / TLS client certificate support to n8n's OpenAI nodes,
enabling connections to OpenAI Enterprise mTLS endpoints and self-hosted
OpenAI-compatible proxies that require client certificate authentication.

### What changed

Five optional fields are added to the existing **OpenAi** credential, gated
behind a "Use SSL Client Certificate (mTLS)" toggle:

- **CA Certificate** — custom Certificate Authority to verify the server
- **Client Certificate** — PEM certificate sent during the TLS handshake
- **Client Private Key** — private key paired with the client certificate
- **Passphrase** — optional decryption passphrase for an encrypted private key

When the toggle is off (the default), the credential is byte-for-byte identical
to today's behaviour. No existing workflows or credentials require any change.

The TLS config is wired through to all three OpenAI code paths:

| Node | How TLS is applied |
|---|---|
| **OpenAI Chat Model** (`LmChatOpenAi`) | Passed as `connect` options to the undici `Agent` dispatcher used by the LangChain `ChatOpenAI` SDK |
| **Embeddings OpenAI** (`EmbeddingsOpenAi`) | Same — undici `Agent` dispatcher for `OpenAIEmbeddings` |
| **OpenAI** vendor node (V1/V2 — text, image, audio, file, assistant, conversation) | Passed as `agentOptions` to `this.helpers.requestWithAuthentication` |

A `normalizePem` helper is added to handle the three PEM storage formats
that appear in practice when users paste certificates into n8n credential
fields: proper newlines (passthrough), literal `\n` escape sequences, and
space-separated single-line format (reconstructed by stripping whitespace from
the base64 body and re-wrapping at 64-character boundaries).

### How to test

1. Set up an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that requires a client certificate
   (or use a local nginx mTLS reverse proxy in front of the OpenAI API).
2. Create an **OpenAi** credential, enter your API key and base URL, enable
   "Use SSL Client Certificate (mTLS)", and paste in the CA cert, client cert,
   and private key in PEM format.
3. Run an **OpenAI Chat Model** node connected to an AI Agent — the connection
   should complete the TLS handshake and return a chat response.
4. Repeat with **Embeddings OpenAI** and the **OpenAI** vendor node
   (Text → Message operation).
5. Disable the toggle and confirm existing behaviour is unchanged.

### Key implementation decisions — offered for reviewer feedback

**SSL fields live in `OpenAiApi`, not a separate credential type.**
The initial approach followed the pattern used by the **HTTP Request** node,
which exposes SSL/TLS options (CA cert, client cert, key) as fields within the
node's own parameters rather than inside the credential. That approach was
considered here — the SSL fields would live on the node itself, matching
HTTP Request's UX exactly. It was discarded for two reasons: first, there are
three separate OpenAI node types (Chat Model, Embeddings, OpenAI vendor node)
that would each need the fields duplicated; second, the TLS material is an
intrinsic property of *how you connect to a given endpoint*, which belongs in
the credential rather than being reconfigured per-node.

An earlier iteration also used a separate `OpenAiSslAuth` credential that nodes
declared as an optional second credential. This was discarded because the
optional credential picker is always visible in the node UI regardless of
whether SSL is needed, which undermines the toggle UX and would require
frontend exemption-list changes (`KEEP_AUTH_IN_NDV_FOR_NODES`). Placing the
fields inside `OpenAiApi` with `displayOptions` gating means they only appear
when the user enables the toggle — no frontend changes needed, and the
credential is self-contained.

**API key stays required.**
The API key field is not made optional. For mTLS-only deployments (no API
key), the user can enter any placeholder string — the server receiving the
request can ignore the `Authorization: Bearer` header. Making the field
optional would be a credential schema change with broader implications and
was considered out of scope for this PR.

**No `skipHostnameVerification` field.**
Deliberately omitted in this PR. The correct long-term fix for hostname
mismatches is a server certificate with the correct Subject Alternative Names.
That said, many real-world mTLS deployments (legacy enterprise proxies,
internal CAs) do not populate SANs correctly, meaning strict hostname
verification will reject otherwise valid connections. If there is community
demand, a follow-up PR can add this as an opt-in field — the undici
`connect.rejectUnauthorized` option would be the implementation path.

**`normalizePem` lives in `nodes-langchain/utils/helpers.ts`.**
A cross-package import from `nodes-base` was avoided. The function is
co-located with the nodes that use it and is exported for testability. If
other LangChain nodes need PEM normalisation in future it can be promoted to
`@n8n/ai-utilities`.

**`TlsOptions` is exported from `@n8n/ai-utilities`.**
`getProxyAgent` is the single point where the undici `Agent` is constructed
for all LangChain AI nodes. Adding the optional `tlsOptions` parameter here
means new nodes get TLS support by passing one additional argument, with zero
changes to the agent factory logic.

## Related Linear tickets, Github issues, and Community forum posts

Community request:
https://community.n8n.io/t/mtls-client-certificate-support-for-openai-credential-covers-openai-enterprise-mtls-beta-self-hosted-auth-proxies/

Reference community node implementation:
https://github.com/JakeBx/n8n-nodes-mtls-openai

title: refactor(instance-ai): Simplify builder working memory template (no-changelog)
body:
## Summary

Replace the 6-section builder working memory template with a compact 2-section preference-oriented template, add admission rules to builder prompts, and give the builder a `list-workflows` tool for runtime workflow discovery.

### Problem

A live audit of an active user's builder memory showed **15,324 chars across 81 lines**, with **8,894 chars (58%)** from `Workflow Topology` and `SDK & Build Patterns` — both fully redundant with runtime tools and prompt injections. This bloated memory:
- Adds **~4-5K redundant tokens** to every builder invocation (injected via Mastra working memory)
- Causes **~50s latency** on `updateWorkingMemory` calls as the LLM reads, reasons about, and regenerates 15K chars of content
- Reduces prompt cache hit rate (bloated memory changes more often, invalidating Anthropic's ephemeral cache)
- Stores stale data (workflow IDs, credential inventories become outdated between invocations)

### Why each section is redundant

| Removed Section | Already covered by | Why memory is the wrong place |
|---|---|---|
| **Credential Map** | `buildCredentialMap()` builds a fresh map at the start of every builder invocation. `list-credentials` tool queries on demand. | Memory stores a stale snapshot — credentials can be added/removed/renamed between invocations, making the cached map misleading. |
| **Node Gotchas** | `@builderHint` annotations in `search-nodes` and `get-node-type-definition` deliver context-specific guidance inline with the node schema. Validation error enhancers catch misconfigurations at build time. | Generic node docs in memory duplicate what's already in the schema. The agent was storing code snippets and parameter docs that are always available via tools. |
| **Workflow Topology** | `get-workflow-as-code` fetches any workflow's current code on demand. In sandbox mode, existing workflows are pre-loaded as JSON files. | Memory was acting as a historical workflow catalog (names, IDs, purposes). Goes stale the moment a workflow is renamed, deleted, or modified. Adding `list-workflows` to the builder's tool set covers runtime discovery. |
| **SDK & Build Patterns** | `SDK_RULES_AND_PATTERNS` — a 469-line block with all SDK rules, code patterns, expression reference, and critical patterns — is injected into the builder's system prompt on every single invocation. | The agent was duplicating SDK snippets from its own prompt into memory. Pure waste — the patterns are literally already in the same context window. |
| **Recurring Errors & Fixes** | Generic build mistakes are covered by prompt rules, `@builderHint` annotations, and validation error enhancers. | Most entries were generic ("always use `newCredential()` not raw objects") rather than instance-specific. These belong in prompts, not per-user long-term memory. |
| **User Conventions** | Nothing — this is the one section that stores genuinely non-discoverable, user-specific facts. | Renamed to **User Preferences** with clearer sub-slots (naming, default trigger, structure, other). |

### Changes

- **Template**: 6 sections → 2 sections (`User Preferences` + `Instance Knowledge`). Only stores what can't be discovered at runtime.
- **Prompts**: Added `## Working Memory` admission rules to both `BUILDER_AGENT_PROMPT` and `SANDBOX_BUILDER_AGENT_PROMPT` — explicit DO/DO NOT store guidance
- **Tools**: Added `list-workflows` to both sandbox and tool mode builder tool sets (replaces persisted workflow catalog)
- **Migration**: Last line of admission rules handles existing users: "If your memory contains sections not in the current template, discard them and retain only matching facts"
- **Tests**: Updated assertions + regression guards for removed sections

title: fix: Preserve `structuredContent` in MCP nodes to prevent AI Agent reasoning loops
body:
# Summary
This PR fixes a data-loss issue in the MCP Client where `structuredContent` from tool calls was being discarded, forcing AI Agents into infinite retry loops.

---

## The Problem
The MCP specification allows tools to return both `content` (text/images) and `structuredContent` (machine-readable JSON). 
Previously, n8n's implementation:
1. **In the AI Agent Tool:** Explicitly ignored `structuredContent`, returning only the `content` array. This forced LLMs (especially OpenAI via the Responses API) to try and parse stringified JSON from text blocks. When the model couldn't find a clean JSON object matching its tool schema, it assumed the call failed and re-invoked the tool indefinitely.
2. **In the Standalone Node:** Only exposed the `content` array, making it difficult for users to access specific data fields without using a `JSON.parse()` expression node.

## The Fix
Implemented a high-performance, type-safe bridge for structured data:
- **Agent Tool (`utils.ts`):** Added priority logic ($O(1)$) to return `structuredContent` directly if it exists. This provides the LLM with the exact JSON object it requires to fulfill its internal schema validation.
- **Standalone Node (`McpClient.node.ts`):** Implemented a merge strategy ($O(K)$) that flattens `structuredContent` into the node's top-level JSON output while preserving the `content` array for human-readable logs.

## Technical Hardening
- **Type Safety:** Added a 4-point guard (`undefined`, `null`, `object`, and `!Array`) to ensure malformed MCP responses cannot trigger runtime TypeErrors.
- **Key Protection:** In the standalone node, the logic ensures that the authoritative MCP `content` array is never overwritten by keys inside the structured object.
- **Performance:** Used shallow copies and reference returns to maintain optimal execution time and memory footprint.

title: fix(ollama): prevent subpath stripping by using robust string concatenation for API URLs
body:
# Summary
This PR addresses a critical URL construction bug in the Ollama node that prevented n8n from functioning correctly when the Ollama API was hosted behind a subpath (e.g., `https://proxy.com/ollama`).

---

## The Problem
The previous implementation used the native `new URL(endpoint, credentials.baseUrl)` constructor.

According to the WHATWG URL standard:
- If the `endpoint` starts with a leading slash (e.g., `/api/chat`), it is treated as a **root-relative path**.
- This causes the subpath in the base URL to be discarded.

## Result
Requests were incorrectly sent to:
`https://proxy.com/api/chat`

Instead of the correct:
`https://proxy.com/ollama/api/chat`

## The Fix
Replaced the native URL constructor with an explicit and robust string interpolation approach:

```typescript
const url = `${credentials.baseUrl.trim().replace(/\/+$/, '')}/${endpoint.trim().replace(/^\/+/, '')}`;
```

title: fix(core): Fix MCP OAuth discovery URL construction and grant type selection
body:
## Summary

<!--
Describe what the PR does and how to test.
Photos and videos are recommended.
-->
Fixes two issues in the MCP OAuth 2.0 credential flow that caused failures with
authorization servers that follow the spec strictly (e.g. Common Room):

**1. `selectGrantTypeAndAuthenticationMethod` throws when `refresh_token` is absent**

The grant type selector required both `authorization_code` AND `refresh_token` to
be present in the server's `grant_types_supported` metadata before entering the
authorization code branch. The OAuth 2.0 spec (and many real-world providers) only
advertise `authorization_code` — `refresh_token` is a token type, not a grant type
that servers are required to list. This caused n8n to fall through all branches and
throw "No supported grant type and authentication method found" even when the server
fully supports the authorization code flow.

**2. Discovery URL construction produces double `/.well-known/` paths**

When the input `authorizationServerUrl` already has a `/.well-known/` path (e.g.
the server URL itself is a discovery document URL, or the fallback path from
`discoverProtectedResourceMetadata` resolves to one), the code was appending
`/.well-known/openid-configuration` onto it, producing a broken URL like:
`https://example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration/.well-known/openid-configuration`

The fix detects when `pathComponent` already starts with `/.well-known` and skips
path-insertion variants in that case, falling back directly to root-level discovery.

body:
## Summary

title: fix(core): Fix unhandled rejection in task broker on runner disconnect
body:
## Summary

When a runner disconnects mid-task for any reason, `TaskBroker.deregisterRunner` runs and deletes both the runner and its tasks from the broker's maps. But the requester may still be processing an in-flight RPC call from that runner that was disconnected and deregistered. So when the requester finishes and sends back the response, `TaskBroker.handleRequesterRpcResponse` calls `TaskBroker.getRunnerOrFailTask` for a task that no longer exists, so it throws an error that becomes an unhandled promise rejection.

This fix skips the `getRunnerOrFailTask` call when we already know the task is gone so we know there will be no runner for it, and `TaskRequester.sendMessage` catches any remaining unexpected errors. Every path that removes a task from the map notifies the requester first, so the requester already knows the runner is gone and the RPC response has nowhere to go.

title: feat(instance-ai): deferred credentials flow for minimum friction builds
body:
## Summary Defer credential setup to **after** the workflow is built and verified, eliminating the pre-build credential gate entirely. ### How it works ```mermaid graph LR A[list-credentials] --> B["build workflow
auto-resolves available,
auto-mocks missing"] B --> C["verify-built-workflow
sidecar pin data"] C --> D{"mocked
credentials?"} D -->|No| E["done ✅"] D -->|Yes| F["setup-credentials
finalize mode"] F --> G[apply-workflow-credentials] G --> E ``` | Scenario | Before build | After verification | |----------|---|----| | All credentials available | None (auto-resolved) | None — done | | Missing → user finalizes | None | "Apply credentials" / "Later" | | Missing → user defers | None | "Later" — saved clean | ### What changed **Data model** — `resolveCredentials()` no longer writes mock markers into `json.pinData`. Instead it returns sidecar data that's never persisted: ```mermaid graph LR A["resolveCredentials()"] --> B["verificationPinData
used only during test execution"] A --> C["mockedCredentialsByNode
stored in lastBuildOutcome"] B --> D["verify-built-workflow
passes as execution param"] C --> E["apply-workflow-credentials
knows which nodes to patch"] ``` **New tools:** - `verify-built-workflow` — runs workflow with sidecar pin data from build outcome - `apply-workflow-credentials` — atomically applies real credentials to mocked nodes **Simplified UI** — old 3-button picker (Deny / Use Mock Data / Use Selected) → clean 2-button layout: **Later** + **Apply/Use selected**. Removed `mockCredentials` from confirmation response, resume schema, API, controller, and store. **Deterministic guidance** — `done` action with mocked credentials now tells the orchestrator exactly what to do instead of "offer to help." **Deduplication** — extracted `buildCredentialMap()` utility, removed dead warning block in `build-workflow.tool.ts`. ## Related Linear ticket https://linear.app/n8n/issue/AI-2236

## Summary
This PR introduces the ability to read all sheets within a Google Spreadsheet using the Google Sheets node's **Get Row(s)** operation. Previously, users had to specify a single sheet or iterate through them manually.

title: refactor(core): Complete migration of subnode generation to unified generator (no-changelog)
body:
## Summary

`code-generator.ts` contained four functions that duplicated logic already unified in `subnode-generator.ts`:

| Old (code-generator.ts) | Unified (subnode-generator.ts) | Mode |
|---|---|---|
| `generateSubnodeCall` | `generateSubnodeCall(…, { useVarRefs: false })` | inline |
| `generateSubnodesConfigForNode` | `generateSubnodesConfig(…, { useVarRefs: false })` | inline |
| `generateSubnodeCallWithVarRefs` | `generateSubnodeCall(…, { useVarRefs: true })` | varRef |
| `generateSubnodesConfigWithVarRefs` | `generateSubnodesConfig(…, { useVarRefs: true })` | varRef |

This PR migrates all call sites in `code-generator.ts` to use the unified generator and removes ~200 lines of duplicated subnode generation logic.

### Safety nets preserved

Two defensive checks from the old `code-generator.ts` were missing in the unified generator. Both have been ported to `subnode-generator.ts`:

1. **`typeVersion ?? 1` fallback** — the old code guarded against nodes with undefined `typeVersion`. The unified generator used bare `typeVersion`, which would emit `version: undefined` for such nodes. Restored the nullish coalescing fallback.

2. **Self-referencing subnode skip** — the old code skipped subnodes where `sub.subnodeName === node.name` to prevent circular references in source data. The unified generator had no such guard. Added the check to both the inline and varRef config generation paths.

### Context bridging

`code-generator.ts` uses `GenerationContext` (with `indent`, `generatedVars`, `subnodeVariables`, etc.) while `subnode-generator.ts` uses `SubnodeGenerationContext` (only `graph`, `nodeNameToVarName`, `expressionAnnotations`). Since `GenerationContext` is a structural superset of `SubnodeGenerationContext`, it passes through directly — no adapter needed.

## Test plan

- [x] `pnpm typecheck` in `packages/@n8n/workflow-sdk` — zero type errors
- [x] `pnpm test` in `packages/@n8n/workflow-sdk` — 86 suites, 9,360 tests passing

title: fix(insights): checklist not reflecting timeSaved settings and dashbo…
body:
## Summary

Fixes two bugs in the insights/time-saved feature reported in #27191. Both bugs are
in the same feature area and reported in the same issue, kept in one PR intentionally.

Also fixes #27268 — same root cause: `hasErrorWorkflow` and `availableInMCP` 
completed state also read from stale `props.workflow.settings`. Extended the 
fix to cover all three checklist items.

**Bug 1 — Production checklist never marks "Track time saved" as ✅**

`hasTimeSaved` computed in `WorkflowProductionChecklist.vue` read exclusively from
`props.workflow.settings`, which is a stale snapshot. After saving settings via the
Settings modal, `workflowDocumentStore.settings` is updated correctly but
`props.workflow.settings` is not synced, so the checklist stayed unchecked until
a full page reload.

Fix: Read `timeSavedPerExecution` from `workflowDocumentStore.settings` first,
falling back to `props.workflow.settings`.

**Bug 2 — Dashboard time saved not updating after executions**

`getInsightsSummary` only queried `InsightsByPeriod`, which is populated by a
compaction job running every 60 minutes. Raw execution data sitting in `InsightsRaw`
(flushed every ~30 seconds) was completely invisible to the dashboard until
compaction ran, causing the `--` display even after successful executions.

Fix: Union uncompacted `InsightsRaw` data directly into `getInsightsSummary` so
the dashboard reflects executions within ~30 seconds.

## How to test

1. Set up a workflow with **Estimated time saved → Fixed → 5 minutes** in Settings
2. **Bug 1:** Save settings → checklist should immediately show ✅ for "Track time saved" without page reload
3. **Bug 2:** Publish the workflow → trigger it → wait ~30 seconds → refresh Overview page → time saved should update

body:
## Summary

When running n8n in multi-main queue mode, disabling a log streaming destination on one instance didn't reliably propagate to the others. The disable action sends a restart-event-bus command over Redis pubsub, but that command was being debounced, which means it could get silently dropped if another pubsub message arrived within the same time window.
This adds restart-event-bus to the immediate commands list so it's processed immediately, without debouncing.

title: feat(core): Introduce expression-based role resolver for SSO claim mapping (no-changelog)
body:
## Summary

Adds the foundational role resolver service for expression-based SSO role mapping (IAM feature, behind feature flag — not yet wired).

- **`RoleResolverService`** — evaluates admin-defined mapping rules against SSO claims using n8n's sandboxed expression engine (`Expression.resolveWithoutWorkflow`). Instance role rules use first-match-wins; project role rules use first-match-wins per project. Failing expressions are safely treated as `false`.
- **`ClaimsContextBuilder`** — builds the `$claims`, `$oidc`, `$saml`, and `$project` context objects that expressions can reference. OIDC merges ID token + userInfo; SAML uses raw attributes. `$project` context (id, name, type, description) is injected per-rule during project role evaluation.
- **Types** — `RoleMappingRule`, `RoleMappingConfig`, `ResolvedRoles`, `RoleResolverContext`, `ProjectInfo`
- Project info is fetched in a single batch query before expression evaluation, keeping DB transactions short and isolated from potentially slow expressions.
- 74 unit tests covering both protocols, ordering, fallback, disabled rules, missing projects, and error handling.

title: feat(instance-ai): add rolling compaction with centralized model registry
body:
## Summary

Closes https://linear.app/n8n/issue/AI-2233

- Adds automatic rolling compaction of older thread messages into a structured summary to maintain long-range context in Instance AI conversations
- New `InstanceAiCompactionService` (CLI) + `generateCompactionSummary` helper (`@n8n/instance-ai`) handle the full lifecycle
- Compaction state stored in thread metadata (`instanceAiConversationSummary`) — no DB migration needed
- Best-effort, non-blocking: failures log a warning and proceed without summary
- Subtle "Recalling conversation..." status indicator via new `status` streaming event
- Context window lookup uses the **Chat Hub model registry** (`context-limits.ts`) — single source of truth covering 100+ models across all providers

## How it works

1. Before each agent stream, `prepareCompactedContext()` estimates the total token usage across all thread messages
2. If total tokens exceed **80% of the model's context window**, compaction triggers on the older message prefix (before the `lastMessages` tail)
3. A lightweight Mastra Agent (no tools, no memory) generates a rolling summary with five fixed sections: Goal, Important facts, Workflow state, Open issues, Likely next step
4. The summary is prepended to the user message as a `<conversation-summary>` XML block
5. System prompt instructs the agent to use the summary for long-range continuity and recent raw messages for exact wording

## Compaction trigger

The trigger is **token-based**, matching the pattern used by Claude Code and OpenAI's auto-compaction:

- **Token estimation**: `ceil(chars / 4)` across all thread messages + 8k fixed overhead (system prompt, tools, working memory)
- **Context window**: looked up from the **Chat Hub model registry** (`maxContextWindowTokens` in `context-limits.ts`), which covers all supported providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Groq, Mistral, xAI, DeepSeek, etc.). Uses exact match first, then prefix match for short aliases (e.g. `claude-sonnet-4-5` → `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`), with a conservative 128k fallback for unknown models.
- **Threshold**: compacts when total estimated tokens exceed **80%** of the model's context window (configurable via `compactionThreshold` parameter, 0–1)
- **Minimum delta**: at least 500 unsummarized tokens required to avoid trivial compaction calls
- **Incremental**: each compaction only processes the delta since the last `upToMessageId`

Example: with Claude Sonnet (200k window), compaction triggers when thread messages total ~160k+ estimated tokens.

## Key design decisions

- **Non-destructive**: raw messages stay in storage/UI — only model input is compacted
- **Token-based trigger**: context percentage, not message count — a few large tool-result messages trigger earlier than many short ones
- **Centralized model registry**: context window sizes are looked up from the Chat Hub's `maxContextWindowTokens` map rather than hardcoded per model family — new models are picked up automatically when the registry is updated
- **High-signal only**: user/assistant text is preserved; tool payloads, binary data, and execution outputs are dropped from the summary input
- **Thread-scoped**: summary is per-thread, not user-global
- **Input order**: `<conversation-summary>` → `<background-tasks>` → user message
- **Status UX**: pulsing dot + "Recalling conversation..." label appears before first token, via new `status` streaming event type

title: fix(core): Fix OIDC/SAML new user provisioning with project and instance roles
body:
## Summary

Fixes a transaction boundary issue where new users logging in via OIDC with "Instance and project roles" provisioning enabled would get a foreign key constraint violation (PostgreSQL) or transaction deadlock (SQLite). The root cause was that user creation and role provisioning ran in separate database transactions — the provisioning transaction couldn't see the uncommitted user row.

- Thread a single `EntityManager` transaction through the entire SSO login flow (user creation + auth identity + provisioning) for both OIDC and SAML
- Make `trx` mandatory on `provisionInstanceRoleForUser` and `provisionProjectRolesForUser` to prevent future transaction boundary bugs
- Add optional `trx` to `changeUserRole` so it can participate in an outer transaction
- Restructure SAML `handleSamlLogin` so all three paths (existing user with identity, existing user first setup, new JIT user) are fully atomic — if provisioning fails, user creation is rolled back
- Add 6 integration tests covering OIDC provisioning (project roles, instance roles, combined) and SAML atomicity (rollback on project role failure, instance role failure, combined failure)

title: fix(core): Fix race condition when stopping jobs in queue mode
body:
## Summary

Fix the race condition on stopping an execution in queue mode where the main process calls `job.moveToFailed()` (which deletes the job key from Redis) while the worker's Bull processor is still running, causing `Missing key for job updateProgress` errors.

To reproduce:

1. Start main and worker in queue mode with `OFFLOAD_MANUAL_EXECUTIONS_TO_WORKERS=true`
2. Create a workflow: Webhook → Code node with `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 120_000))`
3. Publish the workflow and trigger the webhook
4. In the UI, go to Executions → find the running execution → click Stop
5. **Before fix**: Worker logs `Missing key for job <id> updateProgress` and `Missing key for job <id> failed`, execution appears stuck in UI
6. **After fix**: Worker throws `ManualExecutionCancelledError`, Bull moves the job to failed cleanly, no missing key errors

title: feat: Instance AI and local gateway modules (no-changelog)
body:
## Summary

Implements n8n AI, an assistant that lives inside n8n and can build workflows, manage credentials, run executions, query data tables, browse the web, and interact with the user's local machine.

The system is structured as an orchestrator agent that delegates to specialized sub-agents (workflow builder, web researcher, etc.) and streams progress back to the frontend over SSE. Users interact through a chat interface with human-in-the-loop confirmations for sensitive operations like domain access, setup, and file system changes.

### New packages

`@n8n/instance-ai` is the core agent runtime. It contains the orchestrator and sub-agent factory, all tool definitions (~70 tools across workflows, executions, credentials, nodes, data tables, templates, web research, filesystem, and workspace management), the compaction layer for staying within context window limits, domain access gating, working memory, LangSmith tracing, and the prompt construction pipeline.

`@n8n/fs-proxy` is a local daemon that bridges a remote n8n instance with the user's machine. It exposes filesystem, shell, screenshot, mouse/keyboard, and browser automation as MCP tools over SSE. Designed to run in the system tray or as `npx @n8n/fs-proxy serve`.

`@n8n/local-gateway` is the native Electron tray app wrapper around fs-proxy. It handles connection approval prompts, per-capability permissions (filesystem, screenshots, input simulation, browser, shell), and platform-specific packaging for macOS/Windows.

`@n8n/mcp-browser` is an MCP server for browser automation. It connects to Chrome via the browser extension using CDP, exposes navigation/click/type/snapshot tools, and returns accessibility snapshots with every response so the agent can interact in a single roundtrip.

`@n8n/mcp-browser-extension` is the Chrome extension companion that bridges n8n AI to real browser tabs via CDP, using the user's actual profile, cookies, and sessions.

### Backend (`packages/cli`)

The `instance-ai` module follows controller-service-repository pattern. Controller handles SSE streaming, thread management, confirmations, settings, and memory endpoints. The adapter service connects to an external AI service proxy (or uses a direct LLM connection) and routes all LLM/Brave search/LangSmith calls through it. Thread ownership is enforced at the endpoint level. A compaction service manages context window limits. DB entities cover threads, messages, run snapshots, iteration logs, observational memory, resources, and workflow snapshots, all behind a single consolidated migration.
Background task management supports parallel agent runs with per-task trace isolation.

### Frontend (`packages/frontend/editor-ui`)

The `instanceAi` feature module provides the chat experience: `InstanceAiView` is the main view, backed by a Pinia store and a shared event reducer (also used on the backend for snapshot building). Around 50 Vue components handle the timeline, tool call visualization, artifact previews (workflow canvas, data tables, execution results), domain access approval with severity-aware split buttons, credential setup wizards, memory panels, thread management, and markdown rendering. Composables manage SSE event relay, canvas preview state, execution push events, and resource registration.

The chat integrates into the command bar via `useInstanceAiCommands` and the overall AI feature area alongside the existing assistant and chat hub.

### Shared types (`@n8n/api-types`)

Branded ID types (RunId, AgentId, ThreadId, ToolCallId) prevent accidental swaps. The `instance-ai.schema.ts` defines the full SSE event vocabulary and the `agent-run-reducer.ts` provides a serializable state machine consumed by both frontend and backend. DTOs for confirm requests and thread renames live here too.

title: perf(core): Fix slow user mock in cli tests (no-changelog)
body:
## Summary
Excessive use of `mock<User>` is causing exponential slow-down when running our `cli` test suite. This PR addresses that by replacing `mocked` objects with constants, wherever is suitable.

### Context
Jest's `mock()` calls `overrideMockImp` which mutates objects in-place, wrapping nested objects in Proxies. For `User` objects, `GLOBAL_ADMIN_ROLE` is a shared constant with 126 Scope objects. Each `mock<User>({ role: GLOBAL_ADMIN_ROLE })` call added another Proxy layer on top of the existing ones, causing exponential growth in proxy nesting and `jest.fn()` creation.

This is noticeable in `source-control-status.service.test.ts` where first 40ish tests run under 2 seconds, while the rest take around half a minute. Adding more tests to the suite resulted in 30 minute run while running any sub-set of tests in isolation fast fast again.

### Fix
Most straightforward fix is to use constants instead of mocked objects whenever suitable (e.g. where we just need a `User` object without the need to assert or spy on anything within it):

```ts
// ❌ Instead of this:
const user = mock<User>({ id: '1', role: GLOBAL_ADMIN_ROLE });

// ✅ We do this:
const user = { id: '1', role: GLOBAL_ADMIN_ROLE } as unknown as User;
```

title: fix(nodes-langchain): abort in-flight LLM calls on execution stop
body:
This PR addresses **Issue #27185**, specifically the critical bug where clicking "Stop execution" fails to terminate active network requests to LLM providers. Currently, this results in "ghost" executions that continue to run in the background, consuming API credits and server resources even after the user has manually cancelled the workflow. This is a vital fix for ensuring cost-efficiency and system stability in production environments.

#### **Addressing the Reported "Looping" Behavior**
The original issue report mentions two distinct problems. It is important to clarify the node's intended behavior:
1.  **Node executing once per item:** The reporter noted that using `{{ $input.all() }}` triggers one execution per item. **This is standard n8n behavior.** Because n8n is an item-based engine, the node's internal logic fires for every incoming item. To achieve a "run once" result, users should typically use an *Aggregate* or *Item Lists* node upstream.
2.  **Ineffective Stop Button:** The **actual bug** is that when these multiple executions are triggered, they cannot be stopped. The UI shows "Cancelled," but the background network requests ignore the `AbortSignal`. **This PR fixes this specific behavior.**

#### **The Technical Cause**
In `chainExecutor.ts`, inside the `executeSimpleChain` function, the `AbortSignal` was being passed incorrectly to LangChain's `.invoke()` method. 

* **Broken Code:** The signal was grouped inside the input payload object: `chain.invoke({ query, signal })`.
* **Result:** LangChain treated `signal` as a prompt variable to be injected into the text, rather than a system configuration. Consequently, the underlying HTTP client never received the instruction to abort the connection.

#### **The Fix**
Separated the arguments in `chain.invoke()` to strictly adhere to the LangChain `Runnable` interface:
* **Argument 1 (Input):** `{ query }`
* **Argument 2 (Config):** `{ signal: context.getExecutionCancelSignal() }`

This ensures that the `AbortSignal` is correctly routed to the HTTP client, allowing n8n to instantly sever in-flight connections when the "Stop" button is clicked.

### **How to Test**
1.  **Setup:** Create a workflow with a **Code node** (outputting 5-10 items) connected to a **Basic LLM Chain** node.
2.  **Model:** Use a slow-responding model
3.  **Action:** Run the workflow. Once the terminal shows `>>> [DEBUG] 🚀 STARTED...`, click the red **Stop execution** button in the UI.
4.  **Expected Result:** The backend processing should stop immediately. No `<<< [DEBUG] ✅ FINISHED...` logs should appear in the terminal after the stop command is issued.

### **Related Issue**
Fixes #27185

title: fix(core): Use published version for error workflow execution
body:
## Summary

Error workflows were incorrectly executing with **draft (unpublished) nodes** instead of the published version. When a workflow failed and triggered its configured error workflow, the `executeErrorWorkflow` method loaded the `activeVersion` relation but passed the raw `workflowData` entity (containing draft nodes/connections) to `WorkflowRunner.run()`. The runner then rebuilt the `Workflow` from the draft data, ignoring the published version entirely.

**Root cause:** In `WorkflowExecutionService.executeErrorWorkflow()`, the `workflowInstance` was correctly built from `activeVersion.nodes`, but `workflowData` (with draft nodes) was passed to the runner at line 433. The runner creates a new `Workflow` from `data.workflowData.nodes` (draft), not from the already-validated `workflowInstance`.

**Fix:** Override `workflowData.nodes` and `workflowData.connections` with the `activeVersion` values before passing to the runner, ensuring the published version is used throughout.

### How to reproduce

1. Create an error workflow with an Error Trigger node and publish it
2. Create a main workflow that intentionally fails, set the error workflow in settings, and publish it
3. Add a new node to the error workflow **without publishing**
4. Trigger the main workflow in production mode
5. **Before fix:** The error workflow execution includes the unpublished node
6. **After fix:** The error workflow execution only includes the published nodes

title: feat(editor): Auto-redirect to SSO on sign-in page
body:
## Summary

- When SSO is configured as the default auth method, automatically redirect users to the IdP on the sign-in page instead of showing the email/password form
- Adds `?noSsoRedirect` query parameter as escape hatch to bypass auto-redirect and show the normal login form
- Falls back to the normal login form if the SSO redirect fails

## How it works

- `onMounted` in `SigninView.vue` checks if SSO is the default auth method
- If so, shows a spinner with "Redirecting to single sign-on..." and sets `window.location.href` to the IdP URL (SAML or OIDC)
- If the redirect fails (network error, misconfiguration), the spinner is removed and the normal login form is shown
- If `?noSsoRedirect` is in the URL, the auto-redirect is skipped entirely

## No redirect loop risk

- Backend ACS handler renders error pages on failure (does NOT redirect to `/signin`)
- Frontend only triggers on `onMounted` — if it fails, `ssoRedirecting = false` and form renders (no retry)
- If user is already authenticated, the route's `guest` middleware redirects away before `SigninView` mounts

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests for SAML auto-redirect
- [x] Unit tests for OIDC auto-redirect
- [x] Unit tests for `?noSsoRedirect` escape hatch
- [x] Unit tests for fallback on redirect failure

title: fix(editor): preserve stored filter options when resolving typeOptions
body:
## Summary

Fixes #27131

The `watchEffect` in `FilterConditions.vue` merges `DEFAULT_FILTER_OPTIONS` with the resolved `typeOptions` from the node definition but never includes the stored options from the workflow data (`props.value?.options`). This causes user-set values like `typeValidation: "loose"` to be silently overwritten with the resolved defaults whenever an IF or Switch node is opened in the editor.

## Root Cause

In the `watchEffect` block (line ~115), the options merge was:
```typescript
newOptions = {
  ...DEFAULT_FILTER_OPTIONS,
  ...(await resolveParameter(typeOptions)),
};
```

This always produces the node definition defaults. User-persisted options (stored in the workflow JSON) were never included in the merge.

## Fix

Spread `props.value?.options` as the last entry in the merge so stored values take precedence:
```typescript
newOptions = {
  ...DEFAULT_FILTER_OPTIONS,
  ...(await resolveParameter(typeOptions)),
  ...(props.value?.options ?? {}),
};
```

## Test Plan

1. Create a workflow with an IF node
2. Set `typeValidation` to `"loose"` in the node settings
3. Save the workflow
4. Close and reopen the IF node — `typeValidation` should remain `"loose"`
5. Previously it would silently revert to `"strict"`

title: feat(core): Add node that allows checking dynamic credentials inside node
body:
## Summary

  This branch implements the **DynamicCredentialCheck node** — a routing node that checks whether all
  dynamic credentials in a workflow are resolved and available before execution proceeds.

  ### What was implemented

  **New node: `DynamicCredentialCheck`**
  - A routing node with two outputs: **Ready** and **Not Ready**
  - Calls `this.helpers.checkCredentialStatus()` to determine if all resolvable credentials in the
  workflow are configured
  - Routes items to "Ready" if all credentials are available, or "Not Ready" with per-credential status
  details (including authorization URLs for missing OAuth credentials)
  - Gracefully defaults to "Ready" when no execution context is available (e.g., dynamic credentials
  module disabled)

  **Backend: `CredentialCheckProxyService`**
  - New service that bridges the node helper to the credential resolution system
  - Decrypts execution context to extract credential identity
  - Delegates to `CredentialResolverWorkflowService` to check each resolvable credential's status
  (`configured` / `missing` / `resolver_missing`)
  - Generates OAuth authorization URLs for missing credentials so users can complete the auth flow

title: fix(core): Assign webhook ID to API-created webhook nodes
body:
## Summary

When a workflow with a webhook node is created via the public API, we never assign a `webhookId` to those nodes. Without `webhookId`, `getNodeWebhookPath()` constructs the wrong path format, so the registered webhook path can't match incoming requests.

PR #22790 adds `'activate'` to `shouldAddWebhooks()`, but webhooks are already registered during activation on single-instance setups (`isLeader` being `true`). The problem is not that registration is skipped, but rather that registration uses the wrong path because `webhookId` is missing from the node.

Four spots:

- **Public API create** -> Only entry point for API-created workflows.
- **`WorkflowService.update`** -> Assigns `webhookId` to any webhook node still missing one (e.g. workflows created before this fix). Existing IDs are never overwritten.
- **MCP create tool** -> MCP-generated workflows skip the UI. Refactored to use the shared helper.
- **MCP update tool** -> Technically redundant since `WorkflowService.update` now also calls it, but harmless (idempotent). Refactored to use the shared helper.

body:
## Goal (User / Client Outcome)
Enable a non-technical business user (for example, someone in accounting) to safely run approved workflows without editing them:
1. Open workflows they are allowed to use.
2. Understand what each workflow does from creator-provided instructions.
3. Provide required inputs via a guided form.
4. Click **Start**.
5. Get clear output/results while workflow logic stays read-only.

## Use Case
A workflow creator prepares a workflow as an operational tool. A Viewer user then executes it repeatedly with business inputs (text/files) and receives understandable output, without touching workflow internals.

## Technical Scope Included In This PR
- Viewer run mode and role-aware CTA:
  - Execute-only users see **Start**.
  - Run allowed without update/edit permissions.
- Creator-defined explainability and input contract:
  - `viewerMode.manual` in workflow settings.
  - `viewerMode.inputs` schema support (`text`, `textarea`, `number`, `boolean`, `file`).
- Workflow discoverability by capability:

  - Access query handling and validation.
- Creator UX improvements:
  - Guided Viewer Start form builder in Workflow Settings (replaces raw JSON editing flow).
- Viewer post-run explainability:
  - Latest output panel (JSON preview, file keys, empty/error states).
- Hardening and telemetry:

title: feat(core): Introduce CredentialDependency entity to track credential dependencies
body:
## Summary

Introduces a new `CredentialDependency` entity and supporting infrastructure to track which external secret providers a credential depends on.

https://www.loom.com/share/27e084b98d7945aeb4308a1de505de0a

### Changes

- **New `CredentialDependency` entity** (`packages/@n8n/db`): Stores `credentialId`, `dependencyType` (`externalSecretProvider`), and `dependencyId` with a unique constraint and cascade delete on credential removal.
- **DB migration** (`1773000000000-CreateCredentialDependencyTable`): Creates the `credential_dependency` table for both SQLite and PostgreSQL.
- **New `CredentialDependencyRepository`**: Provides `findCredentialIdsByDependencyId`, `upsertDependenciesForCredential`, and `syncDependenciesForCredential` methods.
- **Updated `CredentialsService`**: Parses credential data on create/update to extract and persist external secret provider dependencies.
- **Updated `validation.ts`**: Adds helpers to extract dependency IDs from credential values.
- **Updated repositories** for `CredentialsRepository` and `SecretsProviderConnectionRepository` to support dependency-aware queries.
- **Tests**: Updated and extended tests for `CredentialsService`, `CredentialsController`, and the public API credentials service.

### How to test

**Create flow**

1. Create a credential that references an external secret provider value (e.g. `={{ $secrets.myVault.myKey }}`).
2. Verify a row is created in `credential_dependency` with `dependencyType = 'externalSecretProvider'`.

**Update flow**

3. Update the credential to add a new external secret provider reference — verify a new dependency row is inserted.
4. Update the credential to remove an existing external secret provider reference — verify the corresponding dependency row is deleted.
5. Update the credential to swap one external secret provider reference for another — verify the old row is removed and the new one is inserted.
6. Update the credential without changing any references — verify the dependency rows are unchanged.

**Delete flow**

7. Delete the credential and verify all associated dependency rows are cascade-deleted.

title: fix(core): Emit `leader-takeover` on leadership mismatch in `checkLeader` (backport to release-candidate/2.12.x)
body:
# Description
Backport of #27126 to `release-candidate/2.12.x`.

## Checklist for the author (@ivov) to go through.

- [ ] Review the backport changes
- [ ] Fix possible conflicts
- [ ] Merge to target branch

After this PR has been merged, it will be picked up in the next patch release for release track.

# Original description



## Summary

Scenario:

1. A main is the leader, has `WaitTracker` running
2. This main terminates, and the key still has this main's name, with a few seconds of TTL left
3. This main restarts and tries to claim leadership via `MultiMainSetup.init` during startup. This fails (as expected) because the key is still set, left over from before the restart. This main marks itself as follower
4. `WaitTracker.init` runs during startup. This main is a follower so `WaitTracker` does not start (as expected)
5. The first `MultiMainSetup.checkLeader` runs. This main reads the key and finds its own name left over from before the restart, and marks itself as leader. But importantly, this main does not fire the `leader-takeover` event, because we're assuming that when a main finds its own name in Redis, this is just a routine leadership check
6. Main is now the leader with no `WaitTracker` so waiting executions do not resume

Likely a `StatefulSet` rolling restart on cloud is faster than a restart in the old docker compose setup on internal, and also the hostname is fixed in k8s vs. dynamic in docker compose, where the hostname defaults to the container ID which changes on restart. 

This fix moves `markAsLeader()` and adds `emit('leader-takeover')` inside the existing guard, so the event fires exactly once on the follower-to-leader transition.

title: feat(core): Add execution mode label to Prometheus workflow metrics
body:
## Summary

Adds an opt-in `execution_mode` Prometheus label to workflow metrics (`n8n_workflow_success_total`, `n8n_workflow_failed_total`, `n8n_workflow_cancelled_total`), enabling dashboards to distinguish between production and manual executions.

**New environment variable:** `N8N_METRICS_INCLUDE_EXECUTION_MODE_LABEL` (default: `false`)

When enabled, each workflow metric includes an `execution_mode` label with the run mode value (e.g. `manual`, `trigger`, `webhook`).

**Example output:**
```
n8n_workflow_success_total{workflow_name="My Workflow",execution_mode="trigger"} 42
n8n_workflow_success_total{workflow_name="My Workflow",execution_mode="manual"} 3
```

### Files changed

- `packages/@n8n/config/src/configs/endpoints.config.ts` — new config property
- `packages/cli/src/metrics/types.ts` — new `executionMode` union member
- `packages/cli/src/metrics/prometheus-metrics.service.ts` — wire label into `includes` and `buildWorkflowLabels()`

### How to test

1. Set `N8N_METRICS=true` and `N8N_METRICS_INCLUDE_EXECUTION_MODE_LABEL=true`
2. Execute a workflow manually and via trigger
3. Verify `/metrics` endpoint includes `execution_mode="manual"` and `execution_mode="trigger"` labels

title: build: Pin `uuid` in `n8n-workflow` to catalog version
body:
`packages/workflow` imports `uuid` but doesn't declare it as a dependency. After the langchain packages upgrade at #26892, `@langchain/langgraph-*` brought in `uuid@13.0.0` (ESM-only) as a transitive dependency. When running `pnpm install` locally, pnpm can resolve `uuid` to v13 instead of the catalog-pinned v10, which breaks all  Jest tests in the `cli` package locally with:

```
SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'export'
```

I _think_ CI is unaffected because it uses `--frozen-lockfile` against the committed lockfile which doesn't contain `uuid@13`.

This fix adds `uuid: "catalog:"` to `packages/workflow/package.json` so it explicitly pins to v10.

title: fix(core): Emit `leader-takeover` on leadership mismatch in `checkLeader`
body:
## Summary

Scenario:

1. A main is the leader, has `WaitTracker` running
2. This main terminates, and the key still has this main's name, with a few seconds of TTL left
3. This main restarts and tries to claim leadership via `MultiMainSetup.init` during startup. This fails (as expected) because the key is still set, left over from before the restart. This main marks itself as follower
4. `WaitTracker.init` runs during startup. This main is a follower so `WaitTracker` does not start (as expected)
5. The first `MultiMainSetup.checkLeader` runs. This main reads the key and finds its own name left over from before the restart, and marks itself as leader. But importantly, this main does not fire the `leader-takeover` event, because we're assuming that when a main finds its own name in Redis, this is just a routine leadership check
6. Main is now the leader with no `WaitTracker` so waiting executions do not resume

Likely a `StatefulSet` rolling restart on cloud is faster than a restart in the old docker compose setup on internal, and also the hostname is fixed in k8s vs. dynamic in docker compose, where the hostname defaults to the container ID which changes on restart. 

This fix moves `markAsLeader()` and adds `emit('leader-takeover')` inside the existing guard, so the event fires exactly once on the follower-to-leader transition.

title: fix(core): Preserve nested proxy/redirect shape in log streaming webhook
body:
## Summary

Fixed log streaming webhook proxy/redirect configuration disappearing on reload. The frontend fixedCollection uses the same property name for both the collection and its inner option (e.g., `proxy` → `proxy`), producing nested shapes like `{ proxy: { proxy: { protocol, host, port } } }`. A previous fix used Zod `.transform()` to unwrap this on save, which broke the UI display (frontend expects the nested shape).

Changes:
- Remove Zod `.transform()` to keep data nested throughout the lifecycle
- Add re-nesting in `serialize()` for backward compatibility with legacy flat DB data
- Extract `resolveProxy()` and `resolveRedirect()` helpers to handle both nested and flat shapes when building axios settings
- Add comprehensive tests covering both scenarios

Tested with mitmproxy. Proxy config now persists on reload and requests route through the proxy correctly.
Also tested in case wrongfully flattened config is re-nested on usage or serialization

title: fix(core): deregister crons before re-activating workflow to prevent duplicates
body:
## Summary

Fixes #27103

When a workflow with a Schedule Trigger is saved while active, `ActiveWorkflows.add()` is called again without first deregistering existing cron jobs. Because `toCronExpression()` generates a random second component (`randomInt(0, 60)`) on each call, the new cron expression differs from the old one, bypassing the dedup check in `ScheduledTaskManager.registerCron()`. This results in the workflow executing twice (or more) per schedule interval, with a few seconds offset between executions.

### The fix

Call `scheduledTaskManager.deregisterCrons(workflowId)` at the start of `ActiveWorkflows.add()` to clear any previously registered crons before re-registering. This is a no-op for first-time activations (no crons to deregister) and correctly cleans up stale crons on re-activation.

### How it was found

In production (single main + single worker, queue mode with Redis), the "Redemption payment return" workflow (single Schedule Trigger, every 5 minutes) was executing twice per interval, consistently ~14 seconds apart. The gap corresponded to the difference between two `randomInt(0, 60)` values used as the cron second component.

- Only one workflow entry in the database (no duplicates)
- Only one Schedule Trigger node with one interval rule
- No "Skipped registration for already registered cron" error logged
- Pod restarts did not fix the issue

## Test plan

- [x] Added unit test verifying `deregisterCrons` is called before re-activation
- [ ] Existing `active-workflows.test.ts` tests pass
- [ ] Manual test: create workflow with Schedule Trigger, activate, save/edit while active, verify no duplicate executions

title: feat(core): Apply execution redaction to real-time push events (no-changelog)
body:
## Summary

Applies the existing `ExecutionRedactionService` pipeline to WebSocket/SSE push events
(`nodeExecuteAfterData`, `executionStarted`) so that redaction policies are enforced in
real-time, not just on `GET /executions/:id`.

**Key design decisions:**

- **Copy-on-write redaction** — Adds a `copyOnWrite` option to `ExecutionRedactionOptions`.
  The service checks each strategy's new `wouldModify()` method *before* cloning. For the
  common case (`policy=none`, no sensitive output fields), zero copies are made.
- **Reuses existing pipeline** — Constructs a lightweight `RedactableExecution` from hook
  context and feeds it through the same `ExecutionRedactionService` strategies. No separate
  redaction logic for push events.
- **`wouldModify()` on strategy interface** — New required method on
  `IExecutionRedactionStrategy`. `FullItemRedactionStrategy` always returns `true` (if in
  pipeline, it mutates). `NodeDefinedFieldRedactionStrategy` checks `buildSensitiveFieldsMap`
  and returns `true` only when there are sensitive fields or unresolvable node types.
- **Lazy user resolution** — The `User` (with `role` relation) is resolved once per execution
  and cached across all node hooks in that execution.

title: feat(editor): Use server-side search for project sharing dropdowns
body: ## Summary Converts all `ProjectSharing` callers to use the paginated `GET /projects` endpoint (added in #27036) with server-side search, replacing client-side filtering that loaded all projects upfront. title: fix(core): Prevent credential theft via name-based resolution and permission bypass
body:
## Summary

Fixes two security vulnerabilities that allow users to steal credentials in Community Edition:

1. **Name-based credential resolution vulnerability**: `replaceInvalidCredentials()` queried ALL credentials by `(name, type)` with no project/ownership filter, allowing users to resolve any credential by guessing its name. Now scoped to the workflow's project.

Now included in active type filtering.

title: fix(core): Simplify $items global type declaration in expression runtime
body:
## Summary

Simplifies the `$items` global variable type declaration in the V8 expression runtime.

The previous type `((...args: unknown[]) => unknown) | unknown` is equivalent to plain `unknown` because any type unioned with `unknown` results in `unknown`. This means TypeScript never saw the callable signature, making the union meaningless.

The fix simplifies the declaration to `unknown`, which accurately reflects the runtime behaviour: `$items` can be a function wrapper, a plain value, or `undefined` depending on execution context.

Addresses comment: https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/pull/27015#discussion_r2931923755

title: chore(core): Query executions using a single query intead of two
body:
## Summary

<!--
Describe what the PR does and how to test.
Photos and videos are recommended.
-->
Changed the execution repository query logic when fetching and counting executions 
Why: to prevent db engines errors on the second query when passing too many parameters. 

How: instead of querying first the accessible execution workflow ids from the user context, we pass the context to the main repository function and adds a subquery to filter by the accessible ones

Benchmarks:

**Postgres**
| Scenario | Array (ms) | EXISTS (ms) | Ratio | Verdict |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 20k execs, 10 wf | 7–15 | 7–33 | 1.05–2.19x | Slight overhead, negligible at <33ms |
| 50k execs, 1000 wf | 16–3178 | 13–779 | 0.01–24.8x | Highly variable (PG planner), EXISTS wins big when plan is optimal |
| 20k, 100 wf + status filter | 6–109 | 6–7 | 0.07–0.98x | Faster or equal |
| findLatestCurrentAndCompleted, 20k | 10–27 | 11–19 | 0.68–1.26x | Neutral |
| 20k sharing-enabled, team+personal | 6–114 | 6–8 | 0.07–1.25x | Faster or equal |
| 50k sharing-enabled, 1000 team wf | 14–17 | 13–15 | 0.86–0.93x | Consistently faster |

For the "50k execs, 1000 wf" scenario, In production this is less of an issue because:
- PG has warmed-up statistics from ANALYZE / autovacuum
- shared_buffers keeps hot pages cached
- The planner stabilizes after a few queries

The benchmark creates fresh tables each run with no statistics, which is worst-case for PG’s planner.

**SQLite**
| Scenario | Array (ms) | EXISTS (ms) | Ratio | Verdict |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | :--- |
| 20k execs, 10 wf | 3.34 | 4.72 | 1.41x | Neutral (absolute diff ~1ms) |

| 20k sharing-enabled, team+personal | 3.33 | 3.53 | 1.06x | Neutral |
| 50k sharing-enabled, 1000 team wf | 17.99 | 18.33 | 1.02x | Neutral |

title: feat(core): Preserve streamed announcements and expose announcement step in agent execution
body:
## Summary

This PR improves how the AI Agent handles **streamed announcements (LLM text emitted before a tool call)** during tool execution.

Previously, that text was **not preserved internally**. Once the tool call ran, the agent **lost context of what it had already told the user**. This PR adds optional support for **persisting and exposing that text** in the execution pipeline so that:

* the agent retains context of streamed messages
* users can access that text via intermediate steps
* the agent scratchpad and conversation memory stay consistent with what the user saw

**When does this apply?** Only when **streaming is enabled** on the AI Agent node **and** the new **"Save AI Announcements"** option (see below) is turned on. If streaming is off, or the option is off or left at its default-**the agent behaves exactly as before**; no new step types and no change to how tool calls appear in the scratchpad or memory.

Example use case:

> "Fetching your account data, this may take a few seconds..."

Without this change the agent would have **no memory of having sent this message** after the tool call completes.

---

## Changes introduced

### 1. Announcement persistence (`saveAnnouncements`)

Adds a **Save AI Announcements** option (Tools Agent options, shown only when **streaming is enabled**). Default: **off** (`false`).

When **enabled** (streaming on + option on):

* announcement text is included in the **agent scratchpad**
* announcement text is persisted in **memory**
* the **entire tool call history** is stored for the run

When **disabled** or omitted (default):

* behavior remains consistent with the current AI Agent node
* only the **most recent tool batch** is written to memory
* no announcement steps; scratchpad and memory show generic "Calling tool..." content

---

### 2. New `announcement` intermediate step type (streaming + option on)

When streaming is enabled **and** Save AI Announcements is on, announcements are exposed as their own step type:

```
type: 'announcement'
```

This allows users to:

* inspect streamed LLM output before tool calls
* store announcements externally if needed
* build workflows reacting to agent status updates

Announcement steps are used for **intermediate steps and scratchpad visibility**.

---

### 3. Fix: parallel tool call message structure

While implementing announcement persistence, we encountered an issue where **parallel tool calls produced invalid LangChain message structures** (multiple AIMessages per model turn, leading to tool-call/response mismatch in memory).

This PR fixes that behavior so that:

* **parallel tool calls are always grouped into a single AIMessage** per model turn (one “model” turn with N tool_calls + N ToolMessages), regardless of Save AI Announcements
* when Save AI Announcements is on, that single AIMessage uses the streamed announcement as content; when off, it uses the default “Calling tool…” content
* memory serialization remains valid and announcements integrate correctly with tool call history when the option is enabled

---

## Testing

We tested the behavior with an agent workflow containing **4 tools**:

* **2 tools configured to execute in parallel**
* **2 tools configured to execute in series afterward**

This setup allowed us to validate:

* announcement persistence
* parallel tool call grouping
* sequential tool execution
* memory structure
* intermediate steps output
* scratchpad state

The implementation was also tested using:

**Gemini Flash 2.5 via Vertex AI**

Streaming announcements, tool execution, and memory persistence behaved as expected.

---

## Implementation notes

* **Opt-in when streaming:** Announcement persistence and announcement steps apply only when "Enable streaming" is on **and** "Save AI Announcements" is enabled (default off). At runtime, memory and step inclusion also require both flags-so if a workflow has Save AI Announcements on but streaming is disabled (e.g. after a config change), behavior is unchanged. Non-streaming execution and streaming with the option off are unchanged.

title: perf(core): Make Wait node fully durable by removing in-memory execution path
body:
## Summary

Removes the dual-execution-path behaviour from the Wait node. Previously, waits shorter than 65 seconds ran entirely in-memory via `setTimeout` and were never persisted to the database. This made them invisible to crash recovery, multi-main failover, and the WaitTracker entirely.

**What changed:**
- **Wait node** (`Wait.node.ts`): removed the `< 65s` in-memory branch. All time-based waits now call `putToWait` immediately, regardless of duration.
- **ExecutionRepository** (`execution.repository.ts`): `getWaitingExecutions()` now uses a DB-server-clock-anchored 15-second lookahead window (`NOW() + INTERVAL '15 seconds'` / `datetime('now', '+15 seconds')`) via `createQueryBuilder`. Added `getServerTime()` to fetch the DB server's current timestamp (PostgreSQL: `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(3)`, SQLite: `STRFTIME`).
- **WaitTracker** (`wait-tracker.ts`): poll interval reduced from 60s → 5s. `triggerTime` is now computed relative to the DB server clock (via a 60s-TTL cache with elapsed-time interpolation) rather than `Date.now()`, eliminating inter-instance clock skew from timer precision. Logs a warning when skew exceeds 2s.
- **PrometheusMetricsService** (`prometheus-metrics.service.ts`): added `n8n_db_clock_skew_ms` gauge, scraped live on each Prometheus pull.

**Why:** The 65s threshold existed because the old 60s poll interval made DB-persisted short waits resume late. Reducing the poll to 5s and adding a 15s lookahead window eliminates the need for the in-memory path entirely. The trade-off is up to ~5s of jitter on short waits in exchange for full crash/restart durability.

**Blast radius:** Narrow — only affects time-based Wait node resume and WaitTracker scheduling. No schema changes, no API changes. Safe to revert with a single commit revert; in-flight waiting executions survive revert (they resume ~60s late via the old poll cycle).

**How to test:**
1. Create a workflow: Manual Trigger → Wait (15s) → Set node
2. Execute — verify execution enters `waiting` status in DB immediately (not after 15s)
3. Verify it resumes at ~15s (±5s acceptable)
4. Kill n8n mid-wait, restart — verify it resumes after restart
5. Scrape `/metrics` and confirm `n8n_db_clock_skew_ms` gauge is present

title: fix(community-packages): improve reliability and error reporting for npm commands
body:
## Summary

This PR  resolves a cross-platform compatibility issue affecting npm command execution on Windows. The issue prevented installation of community-packages.

On Windows, `npm` is implemented as a shell script (`npm.cmd`) rather than a raw executable. The previous implementation relied on `node:child_process.execFile`, which cannot reliably execute script-based commands on Windows. As a result, the process failed with an `ENOENT` error before npm was even launched.

This failure was incorrectly caught by a generic error handler and re-thrown as a checksum verification failure, producing misleading error messages such as:

```
Checksum verification failed. Package integrity does not match. Try restarting n8n and attempting the installation again.
```

The fix replaces `execFile` with `cross-spawn`, which properly resolves script-based commands across platforms. The npm execution layer and its associated test suite were refactored to support this change while maintaining full test coverage.

---

## Investigation & Root Cause Analysis

### Incorrect Checksum Failure Reporting

The package verification logic follows a two-step process:

1. Attempt to fetch package metadata through an HTTP request.
2. If the request fails, fall back to a local CLI command:

```
npm view dist.integrity
```

On Windows, the fallback step failed because:

```
execFile('npm', ...)
```

cannot resolve `npm.cmd`.

This triggered an `ENOENT` error which was caught and incorrectly reported as a checksum failure. As a result, users saw integrity-related errors even though npm had never executed.

---

### Limitations of `execFile` on Windows

Many Node.js tools such as `npm` and `pnpm` are distributed as shell scripts (`.cmd`, `.bat`, `.ps1`) on Windows.

`execFile` attempts to execute raw binaries and does not reliably run these scripts.

Alternative workarounds such as:

```
shell: true
```

introduce security risks and performance overhead.

---

### Previous Mitigation

A mitigation introduced on March 3rd (commit `3bc267953a`) improved the error messaging and suggested restarting the application.

While this reduced user confusion, it did not resolve the underlying execution failure. This PR addresses the root cause by ensuring the fallback command executes successfully.

---

## Implementation

### npm-utils.ts

The command execution logic was refactored.

Changes include:

- Replaced `promisify(execFile)` with a Promise wrapper built around `cross-spawn`.
- Ensured reliable resolution of `npm` commands on Windows.
- Captured complete process state including:

```
stdout
stderr
exit code
```

- Improved exception handling so that failures now include the actual `stderr` output from npm.

This enables immediate identification of issues such as registry errors, network failures, or configuration problems.

---

### npm-utils.test.ts

The test infrastructure was updated to support the new process execution model.

Changes include:

- Introduction of `createMockProcess`, a helper that emulates the event-driven behavior of `cross-spawn`.
- Support for process lifecycle events including:

```
.on()
.once()
stdout and stderr streams
```

All existing tests were adapted to the new implementation while maintaining full coverage.

---

## Tests

Automated test results:

```
Test Suites: 1 passed, 1 total
Tests:       50 passed, 50 total
Snapshots:   0 total
Time:        6.879 s
```

Verification included:

- Confirming that `npm` correctly resolves to `npm.cmd` on Windows.
- Ensuring command failures return accurate error messages instead of checksum errors.
- Validating that all existing tests pass without regressions.

---

title: fix(core): Fix custom node icon path resolution
body:
## Summary

Custom nodes installed in `~/.n8n/custom` have broken icons in v2.11.2+. This is a regression of issue #22452, which was previously fixed in PR #23029.

**Root cause:** `DirectoryLoader.getIconPath()` in `packages/core` constructs icon URLs by embedding the raw filesystem path. When `CustomDirectoryLoader` loads nodes using `fast-glob` with `absolute: true`, the `filePath` is an absolute path like `/home/user/.n8n/custom/node_modules/pkg/dist/nodes/Name/NodeName.node.js`. The resulting icon URL becomes `/icons/CUSTOM//home/user/.n8n/custom/...` — an absolute path with a leading double slash.

**Fix:**

1. **`packages/core/src/nodes-loader/directory-loader.ts`** - `getIconPath()` now computes a relative path from `this.directory` before embedding it in the icon URL. The security check (`isContainedWithin`) still validates against the absolute path.

2. **`packages/cli/src/load-nodes-and-credentials.ts`** - `resolveIcon()` now first tries to resolve the URL path as a relative path (the new format). If the resolved path is not within the loader directory (old absolute-path format), it falls back to the legacy behavior for backward compatibility.

**Result:** Custom node icon URLs will be well-formed relative paths, e.g. `/icons/CUSTOM/node_modules/pkg/dist/nodes/Name/icon.svg`, resolving correctly whether accessed directly or through a reverse proxy.

Fixes #26882

title: fix(credentials): skip OAuth URL validation for expression-prefixed values
body:
## What

Skip `validateOAuthUrl()` when the credential URL field contains an n8n expression (value starts with `=`), so expressions like `={{ $env.OAUTH_URL }}` are accepted without error.

Fixes #26940

## Root Cause

`validateOAuthCredentialUrls()` in `packages/cli/src/credentials/credentials.service.ts` called `validateOAuthUrl(value)` on OAuth URL fields (`authUrl`, `accessTokenUrl`, `serverUrl`, `requestTokenUrl`) without checking if the value was an n8n expression. Expressions are syntactically valid at credential save time but fail URL parsing, producing a spurious:

```
OAuth url is not a valid URL
```

## Fix

Added an `isExpression` guard (already exported from `n8n-workflow` and used elsewhere in the credentials layer) to both the OAuth2 and OAuth1 URL validation paths:

```ts
if (typeof value === 'string' && value.trim() !== '' && !isExpression(value)) {
    validateOAuthUrl(value);
}
```

## Tests

5 new tests in `credentials.service.test.ts`:
- Expression values on OAuth2 fields → no error ✅
- Expression values on OAuth1 fields → no error ✅
- Invalid URL on OAuth2 → throws "not a valid URL" ✅
- `javascript:` protocol → throws "must use HTTP or HTTPS" ✅
- Valid `https://` URL → passes ✅

> [!WARNING]
> Some dependencies could not be looked up. Check the [Dependency Dashboard](../issues/18322) for more information.

### GitHub Vulnerability Alerts

#### [CVE-2026-22036](https://redirect.github.com/nodejs/undici/security/advisories/GHSA-g9mf-h72j-4rw9)

### Impact

The `fetch()` API supports chained HTTP encoding algorithms for response content according to RFC 9110 (e.g., Content-Encoding: gzip, br). This is also supported by the undici decompress interceptor.

However, the number of links in the decompression chain is unbounded and the default maxHeaderSize allows a malicious server to insert thousands compression steps leading to high CPU usage and excessive memory allocation.

### Patches

Upgrade to 7.18.2 or 6.23.0.

### Workarounds

It is possible to apply an undici interceptor and filter long `Content-Encoding` sequences manually.

### References

* https://hackerone.com/reports/3456148
* https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gm62-xv2j-4w53
* https://curl.se/docs/CVE-2022-32206.html

#### [CVE-2026-1525](https://redirect.github.com/nodejs/undici/security/advisories/GHSA-2mjp-6q6p-2qxm)

### Impact

Undici allows duplicate HTTP `Content-Length` headers when they are provided in an array with case-variant names (e.g., `Content-Length` and `content-length`). This produces malformed HTTP/1.1 requests with multiple conflicting `Content-Length` values on the wire.

**Who is impacted:**
  - Applications using `undici.request()`, `undici.Client`, or similar low-level APIs with headers passed as flat arrays
  - Applications that accept user-controlled header names without case-normalization

**Potential consequences:**
  - **Denial of Service**: Strict HTTP parsers (proxies, servers) will reject requests with duplicate `Content-Length` headers (400 Bad Request)
  - **HTTP Request Smuggling**: In deployments where an intermediary and backend interpret duplicate headers inconsistently (e.g., one uses the first value, the other uses the last), this can enable request smuggling attacks leading to ACL bypass, cache poisoning, or credential hijacking

### Patches

 Patched in the undici version v7.24.0 and v6.24.0. Users should upgrade to this version or later.

### Workarounds

  If upgrading is not immediately possible:

  1. **Validate header names**: Ensure no duplicate `Content-Length` headers (case-insensitive) are present before passing headers to undici

### minimatch has a ReDoS via repeated wildcards with non-matching literal in pattern
[CVE-2026-26996](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-26996) / [GHSA-3ppc-4f35-3m26](https://redirect.github.com/advisories/GHSA-3ppc-4f35-3m26)

<details>
<summary>More information</summary>

#### Details
##### Summary
`minimatch` is vulnerable to Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) when a glob pattern contains many consecutive `*` wildcards followed by a literal character that doesn't appear in the test string. Each `*` compiles to a separate `[^/]*?` regex group, and when the match fails, V8's regex engine backtracks exponentially across all possible splits.

The time complexity is O(4^N) where N is the number of `*` characters. With N=15, a single `minimatch()` call takes ~2 seconds. With N=34, it hangs effectively forever.

##### Details
_Give all details on the vulnerability. Pointing to the incriminated source code is very helpful for the maintainer._

##### PoC
When minimatch compiles a glob pattern, each `*` becomes `[^/]*?` in the generated regex. For a pattern like `***************X***`:

```
/^(?!\.)[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?X[^/]*?[^/]*?[^/]*?$/
```

When the test string doesn't contain `X`, the regex engine must try every possible way to distribute the characters across all the `[^/]*?` groups before concluding no match exists. With N groups and M characters, this is O(C(N+M, N)) — exponential.

##### Impact
Any application that passes user-controlled strings to `minimatch()` as the pattern argument is vulnerable to DoS. This includes:
- File search/filter UIs that accept glob patterns
- `.gitignore`-style filtering with user-defined rules
- Build tools that accept glob configuration
- Any API that exposes glob matching to untrusted input

----

Thanks to @​ljharb for back-porting the fix to legacy versions of minimatch.
